title: Logo walls and when to skip them
metaTitle: Logo walls and when to skip them
excerpt: Show logos you are allowed to use, at a size people can read, or skip the wall. Gray boxes of famous names you cannot defend are worse than quiet.
alt: A clothing shop interior with folded shirts, hanging jackets, shelves, and pendant lights. The shop display fits a piece about showing only the names you can actually stand behind.
caption: Put on the shelf only what you can explain. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: When should a company skip a logo wall?
faqs.answer: Skip it when you do not have permission, when the relationships are too thin to explain, or when the logos would only be recognizable if you grayed out famous names you barely touched. Quiet is a stronger signal than a row you cannot defend. A single explained project will do more for a careful buyer.

faqs.question: How big should the logos be?
faqs.answer: Large enough to read at the size the page actually ships, including on a phone. A hairline wordmark shrunk to fit twelve in a row is a texture, not proof. Fewer logos, at a readable size, in one color that still has contrast, beat a dense strip nobody can parse.

faqs.question: Is it acceptable to show a client's logo after one small project?
faqs.answer: Only if they agreed, and only if the surrounding text does not imply a deeper relationship than you had. Permission for a project page is not always permission for a homepage lockup. Ask, and describe the work accurately next to the mark. A logo without a true sentence borrows more trust than it returns.

markdown:
Use logos you are allowed to show, at a size a person can read, or skip the wall. That is the rule for logo wall design. A row of gray boxes pretending at famous names you cannot stand behind is worse than quiet. The buyer is not fooled for long, and the ones who check will trust the rest of the page less.

A logo is a borrowed reputation. Borrow it only when the owner agreed, and only in proportion to the work. The layout is the easy part. The permission and the truth of the relationship are the design.

## Permission before pixels

Ask before you place a mark. A contract clause, a written yes, or a brand guide that explicitly allows the use you intend. "We worked with them" is not a license to lock their logo up next to six others under the words "trusted by." Some companies allow a case study and forbid a homepage wall. Some allow the wall and forbid paid ads. Read the line you were given.

Keep the email. When someone on your team refreshes the homepage a year later, they should be able to tell which marks are still cleared. A folder of SVGs with no notes is how a forbidden logo sneaks back in. Treat the permission as part of the asset, the way you treat a font license.

If a client says no, thank them and leave the gap. Do not "forget" a small version in the footer. Do not crop the mark until it is ambiguous and hope. The ambiguous version is still their mark, and it looks sneaky because it is. Replace the slot with a project you can name in public, or with nothing.

When the relationship ends, revisit the wall. A logo can outlive the truth of the work. If they have rebranded, changed hands, or asked to be removed, update the page in the same week. Stale proof is a form of inaccuracy. Google's people-first content guidance treats easily checked factual errors as a reason to distrust a page. A logo is a fact. It should still be true.

## A size someone can read

A logo wall that only works as a blur has failed. The point of a mark is recognition. If you have to shrink twelve wordmarks until they are a gray texture, you have too many, or the wrong ones. Cut until each mark is legible on a phone without zooming. Then look again on a laptop. Legible includes the small type inside a mark, not only the outer shape.

Give every logo the same optical weight. A wide wordmark and a square symbol need different boxes, not a single forced height that makes one of them a speck. Align on the visual center. A strict bounding-box alignment makes circles look like they are floating and wide marks look cramped. This is the craft of the wall. It is also the first thing that looks amateur when it is skipped.

One color, usually the text color or a single muted ink, keeps the wall from screaming in six brand palettes. Muting is not an excuse to drop the contrast until the marks disappear on a photograph. If the wall sits on a busy image, move it to a plain ground. Proof that cannot be seen is not proof.

Do not animate the row, and do not make it an auto-scrolling ticker. Motion hides the mark the person was trying to identify, and it treats customers as decoration. A still row of a few clear logos is calmer and more confident. If you truly have many, paginate by hand or group them by the kind of work, with a heading that says what the group is. A ticker has no heading. It is a refusal to edit.

## When quiet is the better claim

Skip the wall when the logos would overclaim. A famous company that once sat in on a webinar, a tool you use rather than a client you serve, a partner logo you downloaded because the page looked empty: these are the rows that feel like a costume. A careful buyer may know someone at that company. You do not want that conversation.

Skip it when you are early and the honest list is one or two marks. Two readable logos with a sentence each are a beginning. Pretending you have a wall is a middle that you have not earned. The empty state of a young company is a clear offer and a piece of work, not a fake crowd.

Skip it when you cannot say, in one line under each mark, what you did. If the only true caption is "they are aware of us," you do not have a logo problem. You have a proof problem. Go do a project you can describe. The wall can wait. Pages that rank and convert on trust are specific. A mosaic of fame is not specific.

There is a version that is quiet and still useful. Name three clients in a sentence, with the work, and link the case study if it is public. Words can carry a relationship that a tiny SVG cannot. "We redesigned the shop for a retailer" next to the real name, if you may use it, beats a strip of ghosts. If you may not use the name, describe the situation without it. A described situation is honest. A hinted logo is not.

## What a logo does not prove

A mark does not prove the project went well. It proves, at most, that a relationship existed and that you were allowed to say so. The buyer still needs the work, the constraint, or the quote that names the change. Let the logo be a label on that evidence. When it is the evidence, you are asking the buyer to import feelings about a brand that is not yours.

Do not pair the wall with a line like "powering the world's best teams" unless you can defend every word. The logos and the sentence are read together. A modest sentence keeps a small wall honest. A grandiose sentence makes even a true logo look like advertising. Write the sentence first. If it embarrasses you, the wall is doing too much.

Competitors and peers will read the wall differently from prospects. They know who did the work. Overclaiming inside an industry is loud. If the real lead on the project was another studio and you contributed a slice, say the slice or leave the mark off. Shared credit is a sign of confidence. Stolen credit is a story that travels.

Tools, frameworks, and "as seen in" press logos are different walls and should not be mixed into the client row. A Next.js mark is not a client. A conference mark is not a client. Mixing them inflates a crowd and confuses the claim. If you want to show tools, label them as tools. If you want to show press, label it as press, and only where the mention is real.

## Files, color, and the lockup you hand over

Keep a single SVG for each approved mark, named for the company, with the permission note beside it. Do not restyle a client's logo to match your trend. Their mark is their mark. You may set it in one ink for the row. You may not redraw it, add a shadow, or put it in a circle it was never designed for. If their file is a messy export, ask them for the proper one. Tracing it badly is a way of getting the permission and still looking careless.

On a dark page, check the version they allow. Some brands have a reversed mark. Some do not, and a quick CSS filter will ruin the letterforms. If you cannot show it correctly on that ground, move the wall to a light band. The photograph behind a logo row is almost always a mistake. It fights the recognition you placed the mark there to earn.

When a prospect asks "what did you do for them?", the lockup should be able to travel into a proposal with the same sentence that is on the site. If the sentence cannot travel, the wall is only living on the homepage because the homepage felt bare. Put the sentence on the site, or take the mark off.

## Placement, maintenance, and the no

Put a short wall after a claim it supports, not above the headline as a substitute for saying what you do. The first screen should still make sense with the logos removed. If it does not, the logos were doing the explaining and the explaining was weak. Fix the sentence. Then decide if the marks help.

Keep the wall in the same system as the rest of the page. Same max width, same type for the caption, same quiet background. A full-bleed strip with its own gradient looks like an ad unit you sold to yourself. You do not need to sell the idea that you have clients. You need to make the true ones easy to recognize.

Review the wall when you review the homepage, on a schedule, not only at launch. Permissions lapse. Projects get superseded. A logo file from a rebrand will look wrong next to your current type, and it will also be the old company's mark. Assign someone the job of asking, once a season, "are these still true?"

When the answer is no, remove without drama. The page will not collapse. Fill the space with a project story or with margin. Margin is a legitimate design. It says you would rather be quiet than padded. That is a brand position a founder can keep.

Hanabi's public work is a better introduction than a crowd of marks. The projects have names because they can be named. A wall, if it ever earns its place, should be held to the same standard: readable, permitted, and beside a sentence that is true.
